blocks.content: A race condition occurs when two or more threads or processes access shared data at the same time, and the final result depends on the unpredictable order in which their instructions execute. The code can look completely correct and still produce the wrong answer, because the bug lives in timing, not in logic. This chapter builds the idea from a concrete broken example up to the instruction level cause and the general fix.

You will see the classic shared counter race with real numbers, understand why an operation as simple as counter = counter + 1 is not atomic, and meet the critical section, the region of code where races happen. The chapter closes with a second real world style example, the general fix, and how to talk about races in an interview.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415714-693245466.png
1. What Is a Race Condition

A race condition happens when two or more threads or processes touch the same shared data concurrently, and the outcome depends on which one gets scheduled first. Nothing is wrong with the logic of either thread in isolation, the problem only appears because of how the operating system interleaves their execution. Run the same program twice and you can get two different, valid looking answers.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A race condition is a bug caused by timing, where the correctness of a result depends on the order in which concurrent operations happen to execute.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415714-228718499.png
All three ingredients above must be present. Remove any one of them, concurrency, sharing, or the missing synchronization, and the race disappears.
2. The Classic Example: Shared Counter Increment
blocks.text: 2. The Classic Example: Shared Counter Increment

blocks.content: Two threads, A and B, both run counter = counter + 1 starting from counter equal to 0. Run them one after another and the answer is obviously 2. Run them concurrently without protection and the answer can come out as 1 instead, because one increment silently disappears.
The Correct Interleaving
If Thread A finishes its read, add, and write before Thread B starts, each thread sees the other update and the counter ends at 2.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415714-847024360.png
The Racy Interleaving
If Thread B reads counter before Thread A has written its result back, both threads compute 1 and both write 1. One of the two increments is lost even though both threads ran.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415714-481818032.png

blocks.title: The lost update
blocks.content: This exact pattern is called a lost update. It is one of the most common race conditions asked about in interviews.
3. Why It Happens: The Instruction Level View
blocks.text: 3. Why It Happens: The Instruction Level View

blocks.content: counter = counter + 1 looks like one step in source code, but it is not atomic. The compiler turns it into at least three separate machine instructions, and a context switch can land between any of them.

LOAD  R1, counter
ADD   R1, 1
STORE R1, counter
blocks.code:
LOAD  R1, counter
ADD   R1, 1
STORE R1, counter

codes.asm:
LOAD  R1, counter
ADD   R1, 1
STORE R1, counter

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408415714-463709215.png
blocks.alt: Why It Happens: The Instruction Level View

blocks.content: If the CPU switches to another thread right after the LOAD, that thread can read the same stale value. Both threads then add 1 to the same starting point and overwrite each other work.
4. The Critical Section

The critical section is the specific region of code that touches the shared data, in this example the three instructions behind counter = counter + 1. A race condition can only happen inside a critical section, everything outside it is safe by definition.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416406-411947774.png

A critical section is where shared state gets touched, and it is the one place that must never run on two threads at once. The full rules for protecting it are covered in the Critical Section Problem chapter.
5. Why Race Conditions Are Notoriously Hard to Debug
blocks.text: 5. Why Race Conditions Are Notoriously Hard to Debug

blocks.content: Races are timing dependent, not logic dependent, so a program can pass every test and run correctly thousands of times in a row. Then, under a different load, a slower disk, or a busier CPU, the exact same code takes the racy interleaving and fails.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416407-368558914.png
blocks.alt: Why Race Conditions Are Notoriously Hard to Debug

blocks.content: This is why races are sometimes called Heisenbugs, adding a print statement or a debugger breakpoint can change the timing enough to make the bug disappear during investigation. Reproducing a race reliably often needs stress testing with many threads and many iterations, not a single manual run.
6. A Second Example: The Bank Withdrawal Race
blocks.text: 6. A Second Example: The Bank Withdrawal Race

blocks.content: A shared bank account has a balance of 100. Two threads each try to withdraw 80 at nearly the same moment, and each one first checks that the balance is sufficient.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416408-942422482.png
blocks.alt: A Second Example: The Bank Withdrawal Race

blocks.content: Both threads check the balance before either one withdraws, so both see 100 and both see enough funds. Both proceed to withdraw 80, and the account ends up overdrawn even though the check looked correct every time it ran.
7. The Fix: Mutual Exclusion

The general fix is mutual exclusion, a guarantee that only one thread can execute the critical section at a time. A lock is acquired before entering the critical section and released after leaving it, so the second thread simply waits its turn instead of interleaving.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416408-513000151.png

blocks.title: Where the depth lives
blocks.content: This chapter only introduces the idea. The mechanisms that actually implement mutual exclusion, mutexes, semaphores, and the formal critical section problem, are covered in their own chapters.
8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes and the Interview Angle

blocks.content: ["Assuming a single line of code is atomic just because it is a single line in the source file.","Assuming a race that has not been observed yet does not exist, absence of failure in testing is not proof of safety.","Testing only on a lightly loaded machine, where the racy interleaving rarely gets scheduled, then trusting that production will behave the same."]
items: Assuming a single line of code is atomic just because it is a single line in the source file.
Assuming a race that has not been observed yet does not exist, absence of failure in testing is not proof of safety.
Testing only on a lightly loaded machine, where the racy interleaving rarely gets scheduled, then trusting that production will behave the same.

blocks.content: Interview Angle

When asked to spot a race condition, look for shared mutable state touched by more than one thread without a lock, then narrow down to the exact critical section and describe one concrete interleaving that breaks it, the way the counter and bank examples do above.
